bank_ellis.def: First word of a sentence.
bank_ellis.name: <u>Kangaroos</u> are native to Australia.

bank_ellis.def: First word of a direct quotation.
bank_ellis.name: Melinda said, “<u>You’re</u> my best friend.”

bank_ellis.def: A person’s name or nickname.
bank_ellis.name: <u>Peggy</u> likes to be called <u>Peg</u>.

bank_ellis.def: A relationship word used in place of a person’s name.
bank_ellis.name: <u>Mom</u> and <u>Dad</u> went out to dinner.

bank_ellis.def: Initials.
bank_ellis.name: Eddie Trujilo’s friends call him <u>E.T.</u>

bank_ellis.def: People’s titles and their abbreviations.
bank_ellis.name: My dentist’s name is <u>Doctor</u> Olson.

bank_ellis.def: People’s titles and their abbreviations.
bank_ellis.name: My dentist’s name is <u>Dr.</u> Olson.

bank_ellis.def: Names of places, cities, states, roads, and avenues.
bank_ellis.name: <u>Disney World</u> is in <u>Orlando</u>, <u>Florida</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Names of places, cities, states, roads, and avenues.
bank_ellis.name: I live on <u>Fifth Street</u> and <u>Marble Road</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Names of groups.
bank_ellis.name: Jenny is a <u>Girl Scout</u> leader.

bank_ellis.def: Days of the week, months of the year, and holidays.
bank_ellis.name: My birthday is on <u>Tuesday</u>, <u>May</u> 8.

bank_ellis.def: Days of the week, months of the year, and holidays.
bank_ellis.name: We’re going camping on <u>Labor Day</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Titles of books, movies, games, and magazines.
bank_ellis.name: <u>Adventures of Tom Sawyer</u> is a good book.

bank_ellis.def: Titles of books, movies, games, and magazines.
bank_ellis.name: We watched <u>The Chronicles of Narnia</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Titles of books, movies, games, and magazines.
bank_ellis.name: Jesse likes to play <u>Madden NFL</u> with his friends.

bank_ellis.def: Names of planets and stars. (sun and moon are exceptions)
bank_ellis.name: The smallest planet is <u>Mercury</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Names of planets and stars. (sun and moon are exceptions)
bank_ellis.name: The <u>Big Dipper</u> is part of the constellation <u>Ursa Major</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Countries, languages, and nationalities.
bank_ellis.name: When I visited <u>France</u>, I spoke <u>French</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Countries, languages, and nationalities.
bank_ellis.name: My grandparents are <u>German</u>.

bank_ellis.def: The pronoun I.
bank_ellis.name: Malachi and <u>I</u> went fishing today.

bank_ellis.def: First word in the greeting of a letter or e-mail.
bank_ellis.name: <u>Dear</u> Uncle Bill,

bank_ellis.def: First word in the closing of a letter or e-mail.
bank_ellis.name: <u>Your</u> nephew, Jason

bank_ellis.def: Compass points when they name a specific region.
bank_ellis.name: Summers in the <u>Southwest</u> can be very hot.

bank_ellis.def: Compass points when they name a specific region.
bank_ellis.name: Australia is in the <u>Southern Hemisphere</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Acronyms — a word formed from the first letter of a series of words.
bank_ellis.name: Everybody needs some <u>TLC</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Acronyms — a word formed from the first letter of a series of words.
bank_ellis.name: I must do my homework <u>ASAP</u>, or I can’t go outside.

bank_ellis.def: Acronyms — a word formed from the first letter of a series of words.
bank_ellis.name: Dad uses the <u>ATM</u> at our bank.

bank_ellis.def: Period — to end a sentence.
bank_ellis.name: Abraham Lincoln was born in Kentucky.

bank_ellis.def: Period — after an abbreviation.
bank_ellis.name: Fri. Aug. Ln. Mrs. Dr. U.S.

bank_ellis.def: Period — after a person’s initials.
bank_ellis.name: Roger Smith’s initials are R.S.

bank_ellis.def: Question mark — after a question.
bank_ellis.name: Will you wait for me?

bank_ellis.def: Exclamation mark — after a word or sentence that shows strong feeling.
bank_ellis.name: Run! Nanook, run!

bank_ellis.def: Exclamation mark — after a word or sentence that shows strong feeling.
bank_ellis.name: I won the race!

bank_ellis.def: Comma — to separate words in a series.
bank_ellis.name: Raymond likes football, soccer, and hockey.

bank_ellis.def: Comma — to separate the day of the month from the year.
bank_ellis.name: June 25, 2010

bank_ellis.def: Comma — to separate the day of the month from the year.
bank_ellis.name: March 3, 1865

bank_ellis.def: Comma — to separate a street address, city, and state.
bank_ellis.name: Queens, New York

bank_ellis.def: Comma — to separate a street address, city, and state.
bank_ellis.name: 75 Rainier Lane, Rochester, New Hampshire

bank_ellis.def: Comma — in a friendly letter after the greeting.
bank_ellis.name: Dear Susie,

bank_ellis.def: Comma — in a friendly letter after the greeting.
bank_ellis.name: Hi Uncle Fred,

bank_ellis.def: Comma — in a friendly letter following the closing.
bank_ellis.name: Love,

bank_ellis.def: Comma — in a friendly letter following the closing.
bank_ellis.name: Yours truly,

bank_ellis.def: Comma — before a conjunction (and, but, or, so) to join two simple sentences.
bank_ellis.name: We were late, so we missed the concert.

bank_ellis.def: Comma — to separate the speaker from a direct quotation.
bank_ellis.name: Jacob asked, “Where do you live?”

bank_ellis.def: Quotation marks — at the beginning and end of a direct quotation.
bank_ellis.name: “Do your homework,” Mr. Douglas said.

bank_ellis.def: Quotation marks — at the beginning and end of a direct quotation.
bank_ellis.name: Dad asked, “Will you take out the trash?”

bank_ellis.def: Apostrophe — in a contraction, to show where letters are left out.
bank_ellis.name: I didn’t go to school today.

bank_ellis.def: Apostrophe — to show possession (singular and plural nouns).
bank_ellis.name: That is the cat’s food.

bank_ellis.def: Apostrophe — to show possession (singular and plural nouns).
bank_ellis.name: These are my friends’ bikes.

bank_ellis.def: Parentheses — to add information that is interesting but not very important.
bank_ellis.name: Our dog (a poodle) is brown and white.

bank_ellis.def: Parentheses — to add information that is interesting but not very important.
bank_ellis.name: We’re leaving (in my car) to visit a friend.

bank_ellis.def: Parentheses — to surround words or figures to make things clearer.
bank_ellis.name: Patrick earned six hundred dollars ($600) last week.

bank_ellis.def: Colon — to introduce a list of items.
bank_ellis.name: These are vegetables: carrots, celery, and lettuce.

bank_ellis.def: Colon — to separate hours and minutes.
bank_ellis.name: School starts at 7:30 a.m.

bank_ellis.def: Colon — after the greeting in a business letter.
bank_ellis.name: Dear Dr. Bennett:

bank_ellis.def: Semicolon — to join two complete sentences in place of a conjunction.
bank_ellis.name: Caprice stayed after school; she helped her teacher.

bank_ellis.def: Semicolon — to separate a series of items that already contain commas.
bank_ellis.name: The Coos County Fiddle competition winners are Sara James, Coquille; Teri Matthews, Myrtle Point; and John Lynns, North Bend.

bank_ellis.def: Use a before a word that begins with a consonant sound.
bank_ellis.name: Isaac hit <u>a</u> grand slam.

bank_ellis.def: Use a before a word that begins with a consonant sound.
bank_ellis.name: Carlotta has <u>a</u> new puppy.

bank_ellis.def: Use a before a word that begins with a consonant sound.
bank_ellis.name: Maria gave her mother <u>a</u> box of candy.

bank_ellis.def: Use an before a word that begins with a vowel sound.
bank_ellis.name: Jing saw <u>an</u> island out in the distance.

bank_ellis.def: Use an before a word that begins with a vowel sound.
bank_ellis.name: Abraham is <u>an</u> honest man.

bank_ellis.def: Use an before a word that begins with a vowel sound.
bank_ellis.name: I ate <u>an</u> apple and <u>an</u> orange for breakfast.

bank_ellis.def: Use the for a particular (specific) person, place, or thing.
bank_ellis.name: Landau is <u>the</u> most popular member of his team.

bank_ellis.def: Use the for a particular (specific) person, place, or thing.
bank_ellis.name: Bridget climbed <u>the</u> tallest tree in her backyard.

bank_ellis.def: Use the for a particular (specific) person, place, or thing.
bank_ellis.name: Daryl is <u>the</u> only uncle I have.

bank_ellis.def: A common noun is a general person, place, or thing; it begins with a lowercase letter.
bank_ellis.name: The <u>lake</u> was filled with <u>boats</u>.

bank_ellis.def: A common noun is a general person, place, or thing; it begins with a lowercase letter.
bank_ellis.name: The <u>girl</u> wore a blue <u>dress</u>.

bank_ellis.def: A proper noun is a specific person, place, or thing; it always begins with a capital letter.
bank_ellis.name: <u>Toni</u> lives in <u>Alaska</u>.

bank_ellis.def: A proper noun is a specific person, place, or thing; it always begins with a capital letter.
bank_ellis.name: The <u>Great Pyramid of Giza</u> is located in <u>Egypt</u>.

bank_ellis.def: A possessive noun shows ownership. Add ’s to make a singular or plural noun possessive.
bank_ellis.name: Ralph<u>’s</u> bicycle is bright red.

bank_ellis.def: A possessive noun shows ownership. Add ’s to make a singular or plural noun possessive.
bank_ellis.name: The children<u>’s</u> books are downstairs.

bank_ellis.def: If a noun already ends in s, add only an apostrophe (’) to make it possessive.
bank_ellis.name: Ms. Woods<u>’</u> grammar lessons are easy to understand.

bank_ellis.def: If a noun already ends in s, add only an apostrophe (’) to make it possessive.
bank_ellis.name: The lawyers<u>’</u> offices are on the third floor.

bank_ellis.def: A pronoun is a word used in place of one or more nouns.
bank_ellis.name: <u>They</u> went to the library today.  (They = Sue and Jake)

bank_ellis.def: A pronoun is a word used in place of one or more nouns.
bank_ellis.name: <u>He</u> borrowed his sister’s car.  (He = Ben)

bank_ellis.def: Use a noun OR a pronoun, but not both together, in a sentence.
bank_ellis.name: The fly landed on my food.  (not: The fly <u>it</u> landed on my food.)

bank_ellis.def: A pronoun must agree with the noun it replaces. (mountain → it, not her)
bank_ellis.name: The mountain has lots of snow on <u>it</u>.

bank_ellis.def: A pronoun must agree with the noun it replaces. (Bob → him, not it)
bank_ellis.name: Bob won! We were happy for <u>him</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Use a possessive pronoun WITH a noun: my, your, his, her, our, their.
bank_ellis.name: Chelsea is <u>my</u> dog.

bank_ellis.def: Use a possessive pronoun BY ITSELF: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.
bank_ellis.name: Chelsea is <u>mine</u>.

bank_ellis.def: When there is more than one subject or object, put the first-person pronoun (I, me, we, us) last.
bank_ellis.name: Lucinda and <u>I</u> play the piano.

bank_ellis.def: When there is more than one subject or object, put the first-person pronoun (I, me, we, us) last.
bank_ellis.name: Dad tossed the ball to Pete and <u>me</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Use I when you are DOING the action.
bank_ellis.name: <u>I</u> missed the bus.

bank_ellis.def: Use me when you are RECEIVING the action.
bank_ellis.name: Nanook brought the bone to <u>me</u>.

bank_ellis.def: I or me? Add the invisible verb (do): ‘Beth swims better than I (do).’
bank_ellis.name: Beth swims better than <u>I</u> (do).

bank_ellis.def: I or me? When in doubt, leave the other person out: ‘The cat scratched me.’ (not I)
bank_ellis.name: The cat scratched <u>me</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Use myself only after you have used I in the sentence.
bank_ellis.name: I had to prepare the meal <u>myself</u>.

bank_ellis.def: Use myself only after you have used I in the sentence.
bank_ellis.name: I fixed <u>myself</u> a sandwich.

bank_ellis.def: Add -s to the end of most nouns to make them plural.
bank_ellis.name: boat → boat<u>s</u>   ·   flower → flower<u>s</u>

bank_ellis.def: Add -es to nouns ending in s, ss, sh, ch, x (and sometimes o).
bank_ellis.name: gas → gas<u>es</u>   ·   dish → dish<u>es</u>   ·   box → box<u>es</u>   ·   tomato → tomato<u>es</u>

bank_ellis.def: If a noun ends in a consonant + y, change the y to i and add -es.
bank_ellis.name: baby → bab<u>ies</u>   ·   strawberry → strawberr<u>ies</u>

bank_ellis.def: If a noun ends in a vowel + y, just add -s.
bank_ellis.name: donkey → donkey<u>s</u>   ·   monkey → monkey<u>s</u>

bank_ellis.def: Some nouns change completely when they become plural (irregular).
bank_ellis.name: man → <u>men</u>   ·   tooth → <u>teeth</u>   ·   mouse → <u>mice</u>   ·   foot → <u>feet</u>   ·   child → <u>children</u>

bank_ellis.def: Some nouns don’t change at all from singular to plural.
bank_ellis.name: fish → fish   ·   deer → deer   ·   sheep → sheep

bank_ellis.def: Past tense — the action already happened.
bank_ellis.name: Aunt Corena <u>baked</u> my favorite cookies yesterday.

bank_ellis.def: Present tense — the action is happening now.
bank_ellis.name: Aunt Corena <u>bakes</u> my favorite cookies.

bank_ellis.def: Future tense — the action will happen later.
bank_ellis.name: Aunt Corena <u>will bake</u> my favorite cookies tomorrow.

bank_ellis.def: Most verbs are regular — add -ed to make the past tense.
bank_ellis.name: walk → walk<u>ed</u>   ·   open → open<u>ed</u>   ·   start → start<u>ed</u>

bank_ellis.def: Irregular verbs don’t add -ed — the word itself changes in the past tense.
bank_ellis.name: go → <u>went</u>   ·   eat → <u>ate</u>   ·   take → <u>took</u>   ·   write → <u>wrote</u>   ·   become → <u>became</u>

bank_ellis.def: Use a singular verb with a singular subject. (boy → plays)
bank_ellis.name: The boy <u>plays</u> with trucks.

bank_ellis.def: Use a plural verb with a plural subject. (boys → play)
bank_ellis.name: The boys <u>play</u> with trucks.

bank_ellis.def: Two or more subjects joined by ‘and’ take a plural verb.
bank_ellis.name: Rita and Melanie <u>are</u> good tennis players.

bank_ellis.def: Two or more subjects joined by ‘and’ take a plural verb.
bank_ellis.name: He and she <u>were</u> the teams’ leaders.

bank_ellis.def: When two subjects joined by ‘and’ form a single unit, use a singular verb.
bank_ellis.name: Apple pie and ice cream <u>is</u> my favorite dessert.

bank_ellis.def: When two subjects joined by ‘and’ form a single unit, use a singular verb.
bank_ellis.name: Bacon and eggs <u>is</u> a popular combination.

bank_ellis.def: When two subjects joined by ‘and’ form a single unit, use a singular verb.
bank_ellis.name: Peanut butter and jelly <u>makes</u> a healthy sandwich.
